readerTitle: Why does every busy street have five coffee shops?
caseNote: 일상 관찰 (동네 카페 상권) + 가상 적용 (편의점 커피, 원두 로스터리) · 수치는 설명용
insight: 카페의 이익을 갉아먹는 것은 커피 맛 경쟁보다 산업 구조다. 쉬운 진입, 많은 대체재, 강한 임대인이 이익을 나눠 가져간다.
misconception: 커피는 원가보다 훨씬 비싸게 팔리니 장사만 잘되면 카페는 돈이 많이 남는다. 가장 큰 위협은 원두 가격이다.

sources.text: Porter, M. (2008). The Five Competitive Forces That Shape Strategy. Harvard Business Review.
카페, 편의점, 로스터리 상황은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: "원두는 한 잔 원가에서 비교적 작은 비중"이라는 일반 진술입니다. 임대료와 인건비에 비해 작다는 업계 통념에 기댄 표현이므로 구체적 비율은 넣지 않았습니다. 게시 전 업계 자료로 확인하세요.
"원두 공급자(로스터)는 많고 바꾸기 쉽다"와 "좋은 입지는 적어 임대인 협상력이 크다"는 일반적 관찰입니다. 지역마다 다를 수 있으니 단정 표현을 피했습니다.
로스터 사례의 40개 카페, 물량 두 배, 15% 할인은 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: Why does every busy street have five coffee shops?
body: Walk down a busy street and count the cafés. In many neighborhoods there are several within a few minutes' walk.
A cup sells for far more than the coffee in it. Yet many café owners say money is tight. Three forces from this unit explain most of the gap.

image.label: A street with several cafés side by side
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 한 거리에 서로 다른 스타일의 작은 카페 다섯 곳이 나란히 있고, 아침 출근길 사람들이 컵을 들고 지나감. 실제 브랜드 로고나 간판 이름은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your café is busy. What threatens the profit?
body: You opened a café on a busy street a year ago. Lines form every morning and you're making good money.
What is most likely to shrink that profit over the next two years?

options.text: A new café opening a few doors down
options.feedback: This is **new entrants** at work. Your busy shop advertises the opportunity, and little stops someone from copying it.
Bean prices do swing, and it hurts. But beans are a fairly small part of a cup's cost, and many roasters compete for your order.
One customer can't bargain much. The real risk is that they can simply walk to the next café, which brings you back to answer A.

cards.title: Easy to open, easy to copy.
body: Opening a café takes a lease, an espresso machine, some furniture and staff who can learn the job in weeks. None of that is rare. That's a **low barrier to entry**.
So profit sends a signal. The busier you look, the more people think, *I could do that.* Each new café takes a slice of the same morning crowd.
cards.softwareNote: Simple apps work the same way. If a rival can rebuild your product in a few months with standard tools, healthy margins invite copies. Barriers that hold up take years to build, like data, integrations and customer habits.

cards.title: Your rival isn't only the café next door.
body: The customer wants *a hot coffee on the way to work*, or *a place to sit for an hour*. Many things do that job:
list: The free machine at the office
Fresh coffee at a convenience store
cards.callout: **Substitutes** put a ceiling on your price. Charge too much and people brew at home.

cards.title: The convenience store starts selling fresh coffee.
body: A convenience store across the road installs a bean-to-cup machine and sells coffee for much less than you. Some of your grab-and-go customers switch.

options.feedback: The store sells snacks and groceries too, so it can live on thin coffee margins. This turns into **rivalry** on price, a race you're built to lose.

options.text: Lean into what a machine can't offer: seats, skill, regulars greeted by name
options.feedback: You treat the store as a **substitute** and compete on value it can't copy. You may lose some quick sales but keep customers who pay for more than caffeine.

options.text: Add a cheaper basic takeaway coffee
options.feedback: It can keep price-sensitive customers, as long as your regulars don't trade down to the cheap cup.

cards.title: The most powerful supplier isn't the roaster.
body: Many roasters compete to sell beans, and switching can take a phone call. So bean suppliers usually have limited **supplier power** over a café.

The landlord is different. A café depends on its spot, and good spots are few. When the lease ends, the landlord knows moving would cost you your customers. A rent rise can take much of the profit the busy street created.

image.label: A scale: many roasters on one side, one landlord on the other
image.brief: 저울 인포그래픽. 한쪽에는 작은 원두 자루 여러 개("Many roasters"), 다른 쪽에는 열쇠를 든 건물 하나("One landlord"). 건물 쪽으로 저울이 기울어짐. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Now you're the roaster.
body: You roast and deliver beans to 40 independent cafés. A regional café chain offers a deal that would double your volume, at 15% below your usual price, with the right to leave on short notice.

options.text: Sign it. Double the volume beats a lower price
options.feedback: Half your sales would hang on one customer who can leave fast. That's **buyer power**: next year they ask for another discount and you can't refuse.

options.text: Accept only with a longer term, and keep growing the small accounts
options.feedback: You win the volume while limiting how much one customer controls you. Many buyers keep your position as a **supplier** strong.

options.text: Turn it down and stay with small cafés
options.feedback: You stay independent but give up growth that could cut your cost per bag. Often the answer is a better contract, not no deal.

cards.title: The industry average isn't your fate.
body: This analysis explains why the *typical* café struggles. It doesn't say yours must. Some cafés build real barriers: a corner no one else can get, a long lease, a loyal crowd, a brand people travel for.
Use the forces to spot what will squeeze you, then decide what to build against it. Redo the analysis when something changes, like a lease renewal or a new rival.

cards.title: Read the street before you sign the lease.
body: Today you used three forces on one coffee shop:
list: **New entrants:** low barriers mean profit invites copies
**Substitutes:** home, office and store coffee cap your price
**Supplier and buyer power:** the landlord often takes the margin, and one big buyer can do the same to a roaster
cards.callout: **Try it today:** name the one force most likely to squeeze your business, and one thing you could build this year to push back.
